newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Security titans clash in Kremlin rivalry.
newsitem.headline: Security titans clash in Kremlin rivalry.

text.p: The battle between security chief Alexander Lebed and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov began with an air of melodrama in August when Lebed said that Russia was not big enough for the both of them.
Two months later, the clash of the security titans threatens to destabilise a country already shaken by the ill health of the man who holds the reins of power, President Boris Yeltsin.

Lebed, a growling, charismatic general who proved his popularity by coming third in the first round of a presidential election in June, made clear his distaste for Kulikov soon after Yeltsin took him on board to help him through the runoff.
In August, Lebed accused Kulikov directly of dragging out the bloody conflict in the breakaway Chechnya region and challenged Yeltsin via a news conference to choose between them.

"Now I address Russian President Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin: you will have to make a difficult choice. Only one must stay -- Lebed or Kulikov...Otherwise, everything will deteriorate into a fight with a man obsessed with a Napoleon complex," Lebed said.

The 50-year-old Kulikov, whose calm manner and glasses bely his reputation as a hardliner, refused to rise to the bait, confining his return fire to criticism of the peace deal Lebed signed with Chechnya's rebels in late August.
But on Wednesday he got his own back, accusing his bitter rival of plotting to take power in Russia by force.
"The question is what awaits Russia if Lebed comes to power through a creeping coup?" he told a news conference.

The 46-year-old former paratroop general shot back with a sarcastic denial and said he would sue for symbolic damages of one rouble. "There can be no talk of a mutiny," Lebed told Interfax news agency. "The poor thing has got everything wrong."

Yeltsin has taken a back seat role since he won a second term in the Kremlin in July and a Kremlin power struggle has worsened since he announced on September 5 that doctors had recommended heart surgery.

The president, known to favour balancing the various forces around him, has used Kulikov as a foil to Lebed, whose open presidential ambitions and obvious popularity make him a man who must be treated with care.
He has met threats to resign by both men by asking them to stay on and demonstrated his support for each of them in turn.
Yeltsin has not commented on the accusations each has thrown at the other over Chechnya, although he got out the whip on Tuesday to demand the two men settle their differences.
But Kulikov's accusations have now raised the stakes.

He still has thousands of troops in Chechnya -- where a shaky peace has settled in -- and he also enjoys the support of many in the political hierachy who feel Lebed is a dangerous renegade who has sold out Russia's interests.
Lebed has the support of many rank-and-file in the military and has formed an alliance with Yeltsin's shadowy former bodyguard, who once wielded great power in the Kremlin.

"He (Lebed) is actively using his authority as Security Council secretary to create power structures reporting personally to him," Kulikov said. "We have information that he is planning to go on vacation soon to prepare to use force on a local level," he added.

Kulikov said Lebed was planning to set up an elite legion -- a force designed to fight "civil unrest" in the country. Lebed did not deny there were plans for a new mobile force but said they had been discussed with Kulikov and others.
Whoever turns out to be right, it seems that one of them will now have to go.
